issues.legal_issue: The delegated rule-making power to regulate grants of minor-mineral concessions is constitutionally valid because the governing statute supplies sufficient guidance.
material_facts: The State made rules governing quarry and mining leases for minor minerals under a statutory delegation.
The lessees challenged the delegation as excessive and unguided.
issues.conclusion: The delegation is constitutional and does not amount to excessive delegation of legislative power.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 must be read with the statute's public-interest object, the meaning and scope of regulating the grant of concessions and connected matters, the illustrative matters in section 13(2), and the restrictions in sections 4 to 12. Parliament's authority derives from Entry 54 of the Union List, to which Entry 23 of the State List is subject. Legislative history and practice are relevant to interpretation and validity: State of Bombay v. Narothamdas Jethabai and State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley. The illustrative character of particular rule-making topics is supported by King Emperor v. Sibnath Banerjee, Om Prakash v. Union of India, and Shiv Kirpal Singh v. V.V. Giri.

rule.if: minor_mineral_rulemaking_case and statute_states_public_purpose and statute_supplies_subject_matter_guidance and statute_sets_related_constraints

predicates.minor_mineral_rulemaking_case: The proceeding challenges a delegation to make rules regulating grants of concessions for minor minerals.
predicates.statute_states_public_purpose: The governing statute identifies a public-interest purpose for regulating mines and developing minerals.
predicates.statute_supplies_subject_matter_guidance: The statute confines rulemaking to regulating mineral concessions and purposes connected with their grant.
predicates.statute_sets_related_constraints: The statute contains related restrictions and identifies illustrative matters that guide the exercise of the delegated power.

issues.definition: When a minor-mineral rulemaking challenge concerns a delegation confined by a stated public purpose, subject matter, and related statutory constraints, the delegated rulemaking power is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: The power to regulate the grant of minor-mineral concessions includes authority to require payment of rent, dead rent, and royalty.
material_facts: The leases concerned minor minerals and were granted under rules made by the State.
The rules and lease forms required lessees to pay royalty and dead rent, in addition to surface rent.
issues.conclusion: The State's rule-making power includes the power to make rules charging dead rent and royalty, as well as surface rent.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 authorizes rules regulating the grant of concessions and matters connected with that grant. Consideration is integral to a lease under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. Royalty is payment for minerals won from land, while dead rent provides a fixed return based on the leased area. H.R.S. Murthy v. Collector of Chittor describes royalty as payment for materials or minerals won from land. The statutory and historical treatment of mining leases, including section 13(2)(i), the 1948 Act, and the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 and 1960, supports including these charges within the regulatory power.

predicates.minor_mineral_lease_rulemaking_case: The proceeding concerns rules governing grants of leases or other concessions for minor minerals.
predicates.concession_grants_right_to_extract_miner: The concession gives its holder the right to use land and extract minerals for the holder's benefit.
predicates.lease_requires_consideration: The lease or concession requires the holder to provide payment in return for the grant.

issues.definition: When a minor-mineral concession grants extraction rights in return for payment, the rulemaking power includes authority to prescribe those lease charges.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory provision making concession holders liable for royalty does not itself confer the power to prescribe or enhance royalty rates.
material_facts: The statute made a holder liable for royalty on minor minerals removed or consumed by the holder and specified persons acting for the holder.
The statute referred to the rate prescribed in rules made by the State.
The State's power to prescribe the rates was at issue.
issues.conclusion: The liability provision does not confer the rate-making power; that power, including the power to amend rates, derives from the general rule-making provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 makes the holder vicariously liable for royalty on minerals removed or consumed by the holder's agent, manager, employee, contractor, or sub-lessee. Its reference to rates prescribed in rules points to the rule-making power in section 15(1); the proviso separately limits the frequency of royalty increases. Section 9A and amendments made in 1972 concerning other minerals do not determine the scope of the State's power under section 15(1). The contrary view in M.V. Subba Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh was overruled, while Sheo Varan Singh v. State of U.P. and Bal Mukund Arora v. State of Rajasthan were approved.

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_liability_case: The proceeding concerns statutory royalty liability relating to minor minerals.
predicates.holder_is_made_liable_for_others_removal: The concession holder is made liable for minerals removed or consumed by the holder and persons acting for the holder.
predicates.rate_is_referred_to_as_rule_prescribed: The liability provision refers to a rate set in rules made by the State.

issues.definition: When a minor-mineral liability provision makes a holder answerable for specified persons' removals and refers to a rate prescribed by rules, that provision creates liability rather than the underlying rate-setting power.

issues.legal_issue: The State may amend concession rules to increase royalty and dead rent rates even while existing leases remain in force.
material_facts: The leases were granted under statutory rules regulating minor-mineral concessions.
The State amended those rules to increase royalty or dead rent during the leases' subsistence.
The lessees argued that the increases could not affect existing leases or that the power was arbitrary.
issues.conclusion: The State may amend the rules to increase royalty and dead rent rates applicable to subsisting leases, subject to the statutory limits on frequency and other legal constraints.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 includes authority to amend rules, by virtue also of section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The words concerning regulation of the grant and purposes connected with it permit conditions to operate during the lease, including revised charges. A statutory mineral concession is not merely an ordinary contract; public interests in conservation and proper development of mineral resources may prevail over private interests. State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone supports the public-interest approach. A possibility that discretion may be abused does not invalidate the conferring statute, though arbitrary action may be struck down.

rule.if: statutory_minor_mineral_lease_case and lease_was_granted_under_regulatory_rules and state_amends_rules_during_lease and increase_serves_mineral_regulation

predicates.statutory_minor_mineral_lease_case: The proceeding concerns a lease or concession for minor minerals granted under statutory rules.
predicates.lease_was_granted_under_regulatory_rules: The lease was issued under rules made to regulate mineral concessions.
predicates.state_amends_rules_during_lease: The State changes the governing rules while the lease remains in force.
predicates.increase_serves_mineral_regulation: The increased charge is imposed as part of regulation directed to proper mineral development or conservation.

issues.definition: When a statutory minor-mineral lease remains in force and the State amends its regulatory rules for mineral regulation, the increase may apply during that lease.

issues.legal_issue: The State need not provide affected lessees an individual hearing or opportunity to make representations before amending concession rules.
material_facts: The State amended rules to alter royalty and dead rent rates affecting existing lessees.
The governing rule-making provision did not require an individual hearing or representations before amendment.
issues.conclusion: The amendments are not invalid merely because affected lessees were not heard or given an opportunity to make representations.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 contains no hearing requirement. Whether public notice, representations, or legislative approval is required depends on the form of the statutory rule-making power. A court cannot import a hearing requirement that the legislature did not prescribe.

predicates.statutory_rule_amendment_case: The proceeding challenges an amendment made through delegated rulemaking under a statute.
predicates.amendment_affects_leaseholders: The amended rule changes financial obligations affecting existing concession holders.
predicates.governing_rulemaking_power_requires_no_h: The governing rulemaking provision does not require an individual hearing or representations before amendment.

issues.definition: When a statutory rule amendment affects leaseholders but the rulemaking power prescribes no hearing, the absence of an individual hearing does not invalidate the amendment.

issues.legal_issue: Royalty and dead rent may each be increased no more than once in any four-year period measured from the commencement of the governing rules, although both may be increased once in the same period.
material_facts: The governing State rules had a specified commencement date.
Royalty and dead rent rates were increased at different times under successive amendments.
Some amendments attempted a second increase of a charge within the same four-year period.
issues.conclusion: Each of royalty and dead rent may be increased once during each four-year period beginning with the commencement of the rules; both may be increased once during the same period, but neither may be increased a second time in that period.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to section 15(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 bars increasing royalty more than once during any four-year period. The Court applied the same restriction to dead rent, which is related to royalty but is separately calculated and distinct in its basis. The periods are reckoned from the date the State's rules come into force, not from the date of the last increase. The comparable restrictions in sections 9(3) and 9A(2) support this construction.

predicates.minor_mineral_rate_amendment_case: The proceeding concerns an amendment to royalty or dead rent rates for minor-mineral concessions.
predicates.proposed_increase_is_second_for_same_cha: The State has already increased the same charge once in the four-year block measured from the commencement of the governing rules.

issues.definition: If a charge has already been increased once in a four-year block beginning when the governing rules commenced, a second increase of that charge in the same block is not permitted.

issues.legal_issue: A quarry lease for a minor mineral is a mining lease for purposes of the governing statutory scheme.
material_facts: The concessions at issue authorized quarrying of minor minerals.
The statutory definition of mining lease covered a lease for mining operations, and mining operations included operations for winning a mineral.
The State rules described a quarry lease as a kind of mining lease.
issues.conclusion: A quarry lease is included within the term mining lease.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(c) and 3(d) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 define a mining lease by reference to mining operations and define mining operations as operations undertaken to win a mineral. Quarrying is an operation for winning minerals. The Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules also defined a quarry lease as a kind of mining lease.

predicates.mineral_quarry_concession_case: The proceeding concerns a lease or concession for quarrying minerals.
predicates.quarrying_is_done_to_win_a_mineral: The quarrying activity consists of operations undertaken to extract or win a mineral.

issues.definition: When a mineral concession authorizes quarrying to win a mineral, the quarry lease is a mining lease.

issues.legal_issue: A State may classify building stones into varieties and prescribe different royalty rates for those varieties.
material_facts: Building stones were included among minor minerals.
The State classified building stones into different varieties for royalty purposes.
The classification was challenged as an impermissible declaration that the varieties were minor minerals.
issues.conclusion: The State may classify building stones into varieties and charge different royalty rates for each variety.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(e) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 includes building stones among minor minerals, and section 15(1) places rulemaking for minor minerals with the State. The Act does not require a uniform royalty rate for every variety of building stone or prohibit classification for rate-setting purposes.

predicates.minor_mineral_classification_case: The proceeding challenges a State classification used in setting charges for minor minerals.
predicates.mineral_category_is_already_a_minor_mine: The broader mineral category at issue is already included among minor minerals.
predicates.varieties_are_classified_for_royalty: The State distinguishes varieties within that category to prescribe royalty rates.

issues.definition: When an already recognized minor-mineral category is divided into varieties for royalty purposes, different rates for those varieties are permitted.

issues.legal_issue: The earlier royalty amendment was effective, but a further royalty increase and a second dead-rent increase within the same four-year period were invalid.
material_facts: The State's rules had commenced before the amendments in question.
An amendment increased royalty and dead rent during one four-year period.
A later amendment in that same period again increased royalty for certain minerals and dead rent.
The later royalty increase and the second dead-rent increase were challenged.
issues.conclusion: The earlier amendment took effect; the later royalty increase was invalid to the extent it repeated an increase during the same four-year period, and the later dead-rent amendment was invalid because it was a second increase during that period.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(3) and its proviso to the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 restrict royalty increases to once in each four-year period. The Court applied the same frequency restriction to dead rent and reckoned the periods from commencement of the governing rules. Under section 8(1) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and the same principle applied to rules, a reference to a schedule previously substituted is read as referring to its replacement; substitution of the schedule made the earlier amendment operative. The 1974 amendment was valid and effective, the 1975 amendment was void insofar as it increased royalty again in that period, and the 1976 amendment was void insofar as it increased dead rent again in that period.

predicates.minor_mineral_schedule_amendment_case: The proceeding concerns successive schedule amendments setting charges for minor-mineral concessions.
predicates.earlier_schedule_substitution_was_effect: An earlier amendment validly substituted the schedule governing the relevant charge.
predicates.later_amendment_repeats_same_charge_incr: A later amendment increases the same charge again within the four-year block measured from the rules' commencement.

issues.definition: When an earlier schedule substitution is effective and a later amendment repeats an increase of the same charge within the same rule-anchored four-year block, the earlier substitution stands and the repeated increase is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A substantial increase in dead rent is not an unreasonable restriction when assessed together with a corresponding substantial reduction in royalty.
material_facts: An amendment substantially increased dead rent and drastically reduced royalty.
The affected concession holders argued that the increased dead rent unreasonably restricted their ability to carry on business.
The two charges operated together under the concession rules.
issues.conclusion: The dead-rent increase was valid and did not impose an unreasonable restriction when considered together with the reduced royalty.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution protects the right to carry on trade or business, subject to reasonable restrictions. The rates of dead rent cannot be assessed in isolation where the same amendment drastically reduces royalty. Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 authorizes the State to amend the rules, subject to applicable limitations.

rule.if: minor_mineral_lease_rule_amendment_case and dead_rent_is_increased and royalty_is_substantially_reduced_in_same_scheme and combined_burden_is_not_unreasonable

predicates.minor_mineral_lease_rule_amendment_case: The proceeding challenges a State rule amendment affecting financial terms of minor-mineral concessions.
predicates.dead_rent_is_increased: The amended rules increase the fixed charge based on the leased area.
predicates.royalty_is_substantially_reduced_in_same: The same regulatory scheme substantially reduces the charge based on minerals extracted.
predicates.combined_burden_is_not_unreasonable: The overall financial terms, considered together, do not impose an unreasonable burden on concession holders.

issues.definition: When a scheme increases dead rent but substantially reduces royalty and the combined burden is not unreasonable, the amendment does not violate the business right.

issues.legal_issue: A State cannot use a circular to collect royalty at rates inconsistent with valid operative rules.
material_facts: After a High Court ruling invalidated a State amendment, the State issued a circular directing officials to collect royalty at earlier rates.
The Supreme Court held that the amendment setting the applicable rates remained valid and operative.
The circular therefore directed collection at rates different from those prescribed by the operative rules.
issues.conclusion: The circular's directions were invalid and inoperative because the State could not use a circular to charge rates different from those prescribed by the valid rules.
issues.legal_principle: The State's authority to prescribe royalty rates is exercised through rules made under section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957. An administrative circular cannot displace or contradict valid operative rules.

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_collection_case: The proceeding concerns collection of royalty for minor minerals under State rules.
predicates.valid_rules_specify_applicable_rate: Valid and operative rules prescribe the royalty rate applicable to the collection period.
predicates.administrative_circular_directs_differen: An administrative circular directs officials to collect royalty at a rate different from the operative rules.

issues.definition: When valid rules prescribe a royalty rate and an administrative circular directs a different rate, the inconsistent circular is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: An ineffective substitution of a schedule does not repeal the schedule it purported to replace when the intended operation was substitution rather than repeal alone.
material_facts: A schedule prescribing royalty and dead-rent rates had been validly amended earlier.
Later amendments purported to substitute new schedules but were invalid to the relevant extent.
The State argued that the earlier rates did not revive after the later substitutions failed.
issues.conclusion: The earlier valid rates continued in force until they were validly replaced.
issues.legal_principle: State of Maharashtra v. Central Provinces Manganese Ore Co. Ltd. held that a failed substitution is an indivisible and ineffective process, not a valid repeal followed by an unsuccessful enactment, where no intention to repeal independently appears. The same reasoning applied to the substituted schedules in the State rules: the intended substitution did not separately repeal the earlier valid schedule. Section 8(1) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 also supplies a related rule for interpreting references after repeal and re-enactment.

predicates.schedule_substitution_case: The proceeding concerns successive amendments substituting schedules to rules.
predicates.later_substitution_is_invalid: The later schedule substitution is legally ineffective.
predicates.legislative_intent_was_replacement_not_i: The rulemaking authority intended to replace the earlier schedule, not to repeal it independently even if the replacement failed.

issues.definition: When an invalid substitution was intended as replacement rather than independent repeal, the earlier valid schedule remains in force.

issues.legal_issue: The later amendment permitting royalty without dead rent is valid and does not impose an unreasonable restriction when the royalty rates are assessed in the context of the former combined charges.
material_facts: A later amendment deleted dead rent and prescribed royalty rates that were higher than the immediately preceding reduced rates.
The lessees challenged the royalty increase as excessive and unreasonable.
The preceding scheme had imposed dead rent as well as royalty, and the Court compared the new rates with the earlier scheme that included both charges.
issues.conclusion: The later amendment was valid and constitutional and did not violate the right to carry on business; the royalty rates were not unreasonable when considered in the context of the earlier combined charges and the elimination of dead rent.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution permits reasonable restrictions. The rates must be considered in the context of the whole payment scheme, including the fact that dead rent ceased to be payable, rather than compared only with a temporary, substantially reduced royalty rate. Section 15(1) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 authorized amendments to the State rules. The Court also applied the four-year frequency restriction and found the royalty increase to be the first increase in the relevant block.

predicates.minor_mineral_rule_amendment_case: The proceeding challenges a State amendment changing charges for minor-mineral concessions.
predicates.dead_rent_ceases_to_be_payable: The amended scheme no longer requires payment of dead rent.
predicates.royalty_increase_is_first_in_rule_anchor: The royalty rate has not previously been increased during the applicable four-year block measured from commencement of the rules.
predicates.total_charge_is_not_unreasonable_in_comp: The overall burden under the amended scheme is not unreasonable when compared with the earlier scheme that charged both royalty and dead rent.

issues.definition: When dead rent ends, the royalty increase is the first in the applicable block, and the resulting total burden is not unreasonable compared with the former combined scheme, the amendment is valid and reasonable.
